blocks.html:
In Short
  • What I Owned: The combat model end to end: how weapons deal damage, what attacks cost, and the 15 enemy archetypes they're tuned against.
  • Hardest Problem: Making heavy attacks worth their stamina. The model showed that on several weapons, a heavy attack killed in the same number of hits as a light one while costing about 1.7× the stamina.
  • What it Shows: Building a combat economy from first principles, with every number derived from a formula you can audit, and using the model to find problems before players do.

•  A souls-like lives on stamina. Every attack, dodge and sprint draws from the same pool, so weapon tuning is also economy tuning.
  • A toy world with two materials. Enemies are plush or plastic, and the combat had to make that difference matter without new systems.
  • 10 people size in ~1 year of development, so enemy variety had to come from a shared standard rather than one-off designs.

blocks.text: 1. One Damage Formula for Every Weapon

blocks.html:
Every weapon runs through the same three steps, so a new weapon is a row in a table, not new code.


  1. Level scaling: Leveled Damage = Base Damage * (Weapon Level / 10 / 1)
  2. Material split: each weapon converts a share of its damage into Cut (strong against plush) and Impact (strong against plastic). Effective damage is the leveled damage plus the matching share.
  3. Heavy attacks: Heavy Damage = Light Damage * Heavy Multiplier

blocks.html: Some archetypes were later cut for animation or readability limits; mark which ones.

Each weapon leans toward Cut or Impact, so the matchup decides how fast a fight goes. The cutting sword kills a plush Goblin in 2 hits but needs 4 against a plastic one; the hammer is the mirror image.

All combat actions draw from one battery of 200 stamina: a dodge costs 25, a second of sprinting costs 30, and each weapon sets its own attack costs.

Heavy attacks are priced with a single coefficient, Interest:

Heavy Cost = Light Cost * Heavy Multiplier * Interest


Because heavy damage only scales by the Heavy Multiplier, Interest is exactly how much less stamina-efficient a heavy is than a light. At 1.52, a heavy deals its damage at 52% more stamina per point. At 1.20, the premium is only 20%. Interest is the price of burst, and it's set per weapon class.
Damage numbers only matter as hits. For every weapon and enemy, I converted damage into hits to kill and stamina to kill, which is how players actually feel the balance.

• Material reads at a glance. Plush enemies are soft, stitched and fuzzy; plastic enemies are glossy, jointed and hard-edged. Players should know which weapon to bring before the first hit.
  • Every attack is telegraphed. Wind-ups are longer than the dodge window, and paired with a sound cue, so a hit taken is a mistake the player can see.
  • One job per enemy. Each archetype tests one skill: dodging, spacing, target priority, stamina management or weapon choice. Two enemies that test the same skill have to differ in material or pressure.
  • Punish windows match the stamina economy. After a committed attack, each enemy leaves a window long enough for at least one light attack, and big attacks leave room for a heavy.
  • Fits a hit-count band. Enemy HP is tuned to a target number of hits with the right weapon (fodder 2–3, standard 3–5, elite 6–10), so the hit-to-kill model can check every enemy.

Fair in a group. Every enemy has a role in a pack, and a shared aggro cap stops more than two from attacking the player at once.

blocks.text: Iteration Case: Heavy Attacks That Didn't Pay

blocks.html:
Problem: The hit-to-kill model showed heavy attacks were often a trap. In 5 of the 12 weapon-and-enemy matchups, a heavy attack killed in the same number of hits as a light one while costing about 1.7× the stamina. No matchup made a heavy cheaper per kill.

Cause: The model's own check was measuring the wrong thing. It compared the light-to-heavy ratio against Interest alone, but the cost formula multiplies by the Heavy Multiplier too, so every weapon failed the check by design. Meanwhile, the Heavy Multipliers (1.10–1.42) were too small to save a hit on low-HP enemies.

Options Considered:
  • Lower heavy costs across the board. Rejected: heavies would replace lights, and stamina management would disappear.
  • Raise every Heavy Multiplier. Rejected: heavies would trivialise high-HP enemies.
  • Fix the check, then tune heavies by breakpoint. Chosen: measure stamina per kill instead of a ratio, and give each heavy a hit-count breakpoint where it saves a hit on the enemies it's meant for.

Fix: Heavy Multipliers raised on class A weapons so heavies cross the 3-hit breakpoint on plush enemies. Heavies gained a stagger so they pay off against plastic even without saving a hit.

Result: Heavies now save at least one hit in 6 of 12 matchups, and playtesters used them 50% of the time.

One shared formula over hand-tuned weapons. Less freedom per weapon, but every number can be traced and a new weapon is a single row.

Two materials over a full damage-type system. Shallower than elemental systems, but readable at a glance in a toy world, and it still forces a weapon choice.

Stamina as a battery, not regeneration. Batteries make stamina a resource players plan around, at the cost of a slower pace.

Results

  • 6 weapons across 5 classes and 15 enemy archetypes, all driven by one damage formula and one stamina model.
  • A hit-to-kill and stamina-per-kill model covering every weapon-and-enemy matchup.

Looking Back

What Worked: Modelling hits and stamina per kill, not raw damage. It's what players feel, and it caught the heavy-attack problem before playtests did.

What I'd Do Differently: Define each balance check in player terms (hits, stamina per kill) from the start, rather than as abstract ratios.

What I Learned: In a stamina game, every damage number is also a price. Balance the price, and the damage follows.
